title: 10. NLP, Transformers & LLMs: 5.1.4 Subword Tokenization (BPE, WordPiece, SentencePiece)
summary: Idea: Start with characters, iteratively merge most frequent pairs
objectives: Learn how subword tokenization solves OOV
Master BPE, WordPiece, and SentencePiece algorithms
Apply subword tokenization for modern NLP

sections.title: The OOV Problem
sections.body:
### What is OOV?

**Out-of-Vocabulary** = Words not seen during training

```
Visual:

Training Vocabulary:     Test Data:
├── "dog"                "I love dogs"
├── "cat"                      ^
├── "love"                     |
└── "I"                   "dogs" not in vocabulary!
                          Replace with <UNK>
```

```python
# Demonstrate the OOV problem

# Training vocabulary
vocab = {"i": 1, "love": 2, "cats": 3, "dogs": 4, "<UNK>": 0}

def encode_text(text, vocab):
    tokens = text.lower().split()
    return [vocab.get(token, vocab["<UNK>"]) for token in tokens]

# Test cases
test_sentences = [
    "I love cats",           # All in vocab ✓
    "I love puppies",        # "puppies" OOV ✗
    "She adores kittens"     # "She", "adores", "kittens" all OOV ✗
]

for sent in test_sentences:
    encoded = encode_text(sent, vocab)
    print(f"Text: {sent:25} | Encoded: {encoded}")
```

### Problems with Word-Level Tokenization

```
Issues:

1. Large Vocabulary
   English: ~170,000 words → huge embedding matrix

2. Unknown Words
   New words, typos, rare words → <UNK>

3. Morphology Ignored
   "run", "running", "runner" → treated as completely different
   (They share "run"!)

4. Memory Inefficient
   Need embeddings for every possible word
```

### The Subword Solution

```
Key Insight: Break words into smaller pieces!

Word Level:
"unhappiness" → ["unhappiness"] or ["<UNK>"] if not in vocab

Subword Level:
"unhappiness" → ["un", "happi", "ness"]
                 ✓     ✓       ✓
                 All in vocabulary!
```

### Benefits

```
✓ No OOV: Can represent any word
✓ Smaller Vocabulary: 30K-50K subwords vs 170K words
✓ Captures Morphology: Shared roots
✓ Handles Typos: Partial matches still work
✓ Multilingual: Works across languages
```

sections.title: 1 Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
sections.body:
### The Algorithm

**Idea**: Start with characters, iteratively merge most frequent pairs

```
Visual Steps:

Initial: "low" "lower" "newest" "widest"
         l o w    l o w e r    n e w e s t    w i d e s t

Step 1: Most frequent pair? "e" + "s" (appears twice)
Merge: "es"
         l o w    l o w e r    n e w es t    w i d es t

Step 2: Most frequent pair? "es" + "t" (appears twice)
Merge: "est"
         l o w    l o w e r    n e w est    w i d est

Step 3: Most frequent pair? "l" + "o" (appears twice)
Merge: "lo"
         lo w    lo w e r    n e w est    w i d est

... continue until desired vocabulary size
```

```python
# Simplified BPE implementation
from collections import Counter
import re

def get_stats(vocab):
    """Count frequency of adjacent symbol pairs"""
    pairs = Counter()
    for word, freq in vocab.items():
        symbols = word.split()
        for i in range(len(symbols) - 1):
            pairs[symbols[i], symbols[i+1]] += freq
    return pairs

def merge_vocab(pair, vocab):
    """Merge most frequent pair in vocabulary"""
    new_vocab = {}
    bigram = ' '.join(pair)
    replacement = ''.join(pair)
    
    for word in vocab:
        new_word = word.replace(bigram, replacement)
        new_vocab[new_word] = vocab[word]
    return new_vocab

# Example
vocab = {
    'l o w </w>': 5,
    'l o w e r </w>': 2,
    'n e w e s t </w>': 6,
    'w i d e s t </w>': 3
}

print("Initial vocabulary:")
for word, freq in vocab.items():
    print(f"  {word:20} freq: {freq}")

# Run 5 merges
num_merges = 5
for i in range(num_merges):
    pairs = get_stats(vocab)
    if not pairs:
        break
    best = max(pairs, key=pairs.get)
    vocab = merge_vocab(best, vocab)
    print(f"\nMerge {i+1}: {best} (freq: {pairs[best]})")
    for word, freq in vocab.items():
        print(f"  {word:20} freq: {freq}")
```

### BPE in Practice (HuggingFace)

```python
# Using tokenizers library
from tokenizers import Tokenizer
from tokenizers.models import BPE
from tokenizers.trainers import BpeTrainer
from tokenizers.pre_tokenizers import Whitespace

# Initialize BPE tokenizer
tokenizer = Tokenizer(BPE(unk_token="[UNK]"))
tokenizer.pre_tokenizer = Whitespace()

# Train on sample corpus
trainer = BpeTrainer(
    vocab_size=100,
    special_tokens=["[UNK]", "[PAD]", "[CLS]", "[SEP]", "[MASK]"]
)

# Sample texts
texts = [
    "This is a sample sentence.",
    "Another sentence for training.",
    "Machine learning is fascinating.",
    "Natural language processing rocks!"
]

# Train
tokenizer.train_from_iterator(texts, trainer=trainer)

# Test tokenization
test_text = "This is machine learning!"
encoding = tokenizer.encode(test_text)

print(f"Original: {test_text}")
print(f"Tokens: {encoding.tokens}")
print(f"Token IDs: {encoding.ids}")
```

### BPE with GPT-2 Tokenizer

```python
# GPT-2 uses BPE
from transformers import GPT2Tokenizer

tokenizer = GPT2Tokenizer.from_pretrained('gpt2')

# Test texts
texts = [
    "Hello world",
    "unhappiness",
    "antidisestablishmentarianism",
    "COVID-19",
    "supercalifragilisticexpialidocious"
]

for text in texts:
    tokens = tokenizer.tokenize(text)
    print(f"Text: {text:40} | Tokens: {tokens}")
```

sections.title: 2 WordPiece
sections.body:
### How WordPiece Differs from BPE

```
BPE:       Merge based on frequency
WordPiece: Merge based on likelihood (probability-based)

WordPiece Score = (freq(AB)) / (freq(A) × freq(B))

Intuition: Merge pairs that are more likely to occur together
           than by chance
```

### WordPiece Notation

```
Word: "unhappiness"

Tokenized: ["un", "##happi", "##ness"]
                   ^^          ^^
                   ## = continuation marker
```

```python
# WordPiece with BERT tokenizer
from transformers import BertTokenizer

tokenizer = BertTokenizer.from_pretrained('bert-base-uncased')

# Test texts
texts = [
    "unhappiness",
    "preprocessing",
    "antidisestablishmentarianism",
    "playing",
    "unbelievable"
]

print("WordPiece Tokenization (BERT):")
for text in texts:
    tokens = tokenizer.tokenize(text)
    print(f"Text: {text:35} | Tokens: {tokens}")

# Detailed view
print("\nDetailed encoding:")
text = "unhappiness"
encoding = tokenizer(text, return_tensors='pt')
print(f"Text: {text}")
print(f"Tokens: {tokenizer.tokenize(text)}")
print(f"Token IDs: {encoding['input_ids']}")
print(f"Decoded: {tokenizer.decode(encoding['input_ids'][0])}")
```

### Visual Comparison: BPE vs WordPiece

```
Text: "playing"

GPT-2 (BPE):       ["play", "ing"]
BERT (WordPiece):  ["play", "##ing"]
                             ^^
                        Continuation marker
```

```python
# Compare BPE vs WordPiece
gpt2_tokenizer = GPT2Tokenizer.from_pretrained('gpt2')
bert_tokenizer = BertTokenizer.from_pretrained('bert-base-uncased')

test_words = [
    "playing",
    "unhappiness",
    "preprocessing",
    "unbelievable"
]

print("BPE vs WordPiece Comparison:")
print("-" * 80)
for word in test_words:
    gpt2_tokens = gpt2_tokenizer.tokenize(word)
    bert_tokens = bert_tokenizer.tokenize(word)
    
    print(f"Word: {word:20}")
    print(f"  GPT-2 (BPE):      {gpt2_tokens}")
    print(f"  BERT (WordPiece): {bert_tokens}")
    print()
```

sections.title: 3 SentencePiece
sections.body:
### What Makes SentencePiece Special?

```
Traditional Tokenizers:
  Raw Text → Pre-tokenization (whitespace) → Subword tokenization

SentencePiece:
  Raw Text → Subword tokenization (treats text as raw bytes)
  
Benefits:
✓ Language-agnostic (no whitespace assumption)
✓ Works for Chinese, Japanese (no spaces)
✓ Treats spaces as regular characters
✓ Reversible (can reconstruct original)
```

```python
# Install sentencepiece if needed
# !pip install sentencepiece

import sentencepiece as spm
import tempfile
import os

# Create sample corpus
corpus = """
Natural language processing is fascinating.
Machine learning models need tokenization.
Subword tokenization solves the OOV problem.
Deep learning transformers use subwords.
"""

# Save corpus to temp file
with tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile(mode='w', delete=False, suffix='.txt') as f:
    f.write(corpus)
    corpus_file = f.name

# Train SentencePiece model
model_prefix = 'sp_model'
spm.SentencePieceTrainer.train(
    input=corpus_file,
    model_prefix=model_prefix,
    vocab_size=100,
    model_type='bpe'  # or 'unigram'
)

# Load trained model
sp = spm.SentencePieceProcessor()
sp.load(f'{model_prefix}.model')

# Test tokenization
texts = [
    "Natural language processing",
    "Machine learning",
    "Tokenization is important"
]

print("SentencePiece Tokenization:")
for text in texts:
    tokens = sp.encode_as_pieces(text)
    ids = sp.encode_as_ids(text)
    print(f"Text: {text:35}")
    print(f"  Tokens: {tokens}")
    print(f"  IDs: {ids}")
    print()

# Cleanup
os.remove(corpus_file)
os.remove(f'{model_prefix}.model')
os.remove(f'{model_prefix}.vocab')
```

### SentencePiece Special Feature: Space as Underscore

```
Input: "Hello world"

SentencePiece: ["▁Hello", "▁world"]
                ^
                ▁ = space character (U+2581)

This allows perfect reconstruction:
"▁Hello" + "▁world" → "Hello world"
```

```python
# SentencePiece with T5 tokenizer (uses SentencePiece)
from transformers import T5Tokenizer

tokenizer = T5Tokenizer.from_pretrained('t5-small')

texts = [
    "Hello world",
    "Natural language processing",
    "Machine learning is amazing"
]

print("T5 (SentencePiece) Tokenization:")
for text in texts:
    tokens = tokenizer.tokenize(text)
    print(f"Text: {text:35} | Tokens: {tokens}")
    
# Notice the ▁ character for spaces!
print("\nDetailed view:")
text = "Hello world"
tokens = tokenizer.tokenize(text)
for i, token in enumerate(tokens):
    print(f"Token {i}: '{token}' (space: {token.startswith('▁')})")
```

sections.title: 4 Comprehensive Comparison
sections.body:
### Algorithm Comparison

```
┌─────────────┬──────────────┬──────────────┬──────────────────┐
│  Algorithm  │   Strategy   │  Pre-split   │   Used By        │
├─────────────┼──────────────┼──────────────┼──────────────────┤
│    BPE      │  Frequency   │     Yes      │  GPT-2, RoBERTa  │
│ WordPiece   │ Likelihood   │     Yes      │  BERT            │
│SentencePiece│ Unigram/BPE  │      No      │  T5, XLNet       │
└─────────────┴──────────────┴──────────────┴──────────────────┘
```

```python
# Load different tokenizers
from transformers import (
    GPT2Tokenizer,
    BertTokenizer,
    T5Tokenizer,
    RobertaTokenizer
)

tokenizers = {
    'GPT-2 (BPE)': GPT2Tokenizer.from_pretrained('gpt2'),
    'BERT (WordPiece)': BertTokenizer.from_pretrained('bert-base-uncased'),
    'T5 (SentencePiece)': T5Tokenizer.from_pretrained('t5-small'),
    'RoBERTa (BPE)': RobertaTokenizer.from_pretrained('roberta-base')
}

# Test on various texts
test_texts = [
    "Hello world!",
    "unhappiness",
    "COVID-19",
    "Machine learning"
]

for text in test_texts:
    print(f"\nText: {text}")
    print("-" * 80)
    for name, tokenizer in tokenizers.items():
        try:
            tokens = tokenizer.tokenize(text)
            print(f"{name:25} | {tokens}")
        except Exception as e:
            print(f"{name:25} | Error: {e}")
```

sections.title: 5 Practical Applications
sections.body:
### Handling Rare Words

```python
# Compare word-level vs subword on rare words
from transformers import GPT2Tokenizer

tokenizer = GPT2Tokenizer.from_pretrained('gpt2')

# Rare/made-up words
rare_words = [
    "supercalifragilisticexpialidocious",
    "pneumonoultramicroscopicsilicovolcanoconiosis",
    "floccinaucinihilipilification",
    "antidisestablishmentarianism"
]

print("Rare Word Tokenization:")
for word in rare_words:
    tokens = tokenizer.tokenize(word)
    print(f"Word: {word:50}")
    print(f"  Tokens: {tokens}")
    print(f"  # Tokens: {len(tokens)}")
    print()
```

### Multilingual Support

```python
# Test multilingual capabilities
from transformers import XLMRobertaTokenizer

tokenizer = XLMRobertaTokenizer.from_pretrained('xlm-roberta-base')

# Different languages
multilingual_texts = [
    ("Hello world", "English"),
    ("Bonjour le monde", "French"),
    ("Hola mundo", "Spanish"),
    ("你好世界", "Chinese"),
    ("こんにちは世界", "Japanese"),
    ("مرحبا بالعالم", "Arabic")
]

print("Multilingual Tokenization:")
for text, lang in multilingual_texts:
    tokens = tokenizer.tokenize(text)
    print(f"{lang:10} | Text: {text:20} | Tokens: {tokens}")
```

sections.title: Key Takeaways
sections.body:
### Subword Tokenization Benefits

```
✓ No OOV Problem
  Any word can be represented (worst case: characters)

✓ Smaller Vocabulary
  30K-50K subwords vs 100K+ words

✓ Shared Morphology
  "happy", "unhappy", "happiness" share "happi"

✓ Handles Rare Words
  Break into known pieces

✓ Multilingual Support
  Works across languages
```

### Algorithm Selection Guide

```
Use BPE when:
├── Standard transformer models (GPT)
├── General text generation
└── English/European languages

Use WordPiece when:
├── BERT-style models
├── Classification tasks
└── Need continuation markers

Use SentencePiece when:
├── Multilingual models
├── Languages without spaces (Chinese, Japanese)
├── Need reversible tokenization
└── T5-style models
```

### Best Practices

```
✓ DO:
  • Match tokenizer to model architecture
  • Use pre-trained tokenizers when possible
  • Consider domain-specific training
  • Test on your specific data
  • Monitor token length (affects inference speed)

✗ DON'T:
  • Mix tokenizers between training and inference
  • Use arbitrary vocabulary sizes
  • Ignore special tokens ([CLS], [SEP], etc.)
  • Forget to handle padding and truncation
```
